controls.statement: Every critical journey passes positive, negative, boundary, invalid-input, empty-state, maximum-size, and high-volume tests.
Duplicate submissions, refreshes, retries, browser navigation, and network interruption do not create unintended duplicate effects or corrupt state.
Race conditions are tested around balances, inventory, permissions, limits, quotas, and state transitions.
Invalid state-transition ordering is rejected.
Partial failures cannot leave ambiguous or silently inconsistent results.
Eventually consistent operations expose correct pending, completed, and failed states.
Reconciliation detects missing, duplicated, and mismatched records.
Money uses correct decimal, currency, tax, exchange-rate, and rounding behavior.
Unicode, normalization, collation, case behavior, and confusable characters do not create duplicates or bypasses.
Limits and quotas are enforced at a trusted server-side boundary.
Approval and multi-person authorization workflows cannot be bypassed.
Suspension and termination affect all relevant sessions, tokens, workers, integrations, and cached permissions.
Long-running operations resume safely or fail clearly.
Scheduled jobs handle missed runs, overlap, retry, and duplicate execution.
Background jobs preserve correct user, authorization, and tenant context.
Dead-lettered work can be inspected and replayed safely.
Support tools cannot create unsupported or impossible states.
Error messages provide a safe, actionable next step without exposing sensitive details.
All untrusted input sources are identified.

Architecture, data flow, dependencies, deployment, recovery, and local setup are documented.
Build, test, migration, deployment, and troubleshooting commands are documented.
Coding, review, testing, security, release, and support conventions are documented.
Critical code and systems have appropriate maintainers.
Complexity, coupling, and operational burden are reviewed.
Dead code, obsolete paths, stale flags, and unsupported compatibility layers are removed.
Runtime, platform, protocol, certificate, and dependency end-of-support dates are tracked.
Technical debt affecting reliability, security, privacy, accessibility, or operability is recorded.
API, data, feature, and client deprecation policies exist.
Support personnel are trained on released behavior.
Known issues and limitations are communicated accurately.
Maintenance windows and communications are defined.
Decommissioning, end-of-service export, retention, archival, and secure deletion have documented plans.
Make code behavior satisfy explicit requirements and preserve documented invariants.
Choose representations, algorithms, and control flow that make correctness apparent.
Keep units small enough to understand while preserving cohesive behavior.
Use clear names that reflect domain meaning, units, ownership, and side effects.
Prefer explicit data flow, dependencies, state transitions, and error paths.
Avoid surprising implicit conversion, mutation, global state, order dependence, and hidden I/O.
Validate untrusted input at trust boundaries and preserve validated types internally.
Keep authorization, privacy, safety, and business rules in enforceable trusted locations.
Handle every resource, transaction, lock, stream, handle, and subscription through a defined lifecycle.
Use abstractions only when they reduce total understanding and change cost.
Keep comments focused on intent, constraints, trade-offs, and non-obvious reasons rather than restating syntax.
Delete unreachable, obsolete, duplicated, debug, and commented-out code.
Treat warnings, static-analysis findings, and undefined behavior according to an explicit policy.
Make exceptional and degraded behavior deliberate rather than accidental fall-through.
Use deterministic behavior where nondeterminism is not required.
Avoid unbounded recursion, allocation, concurrency, retries, queues, and input size.
Make important behavior observable without logging secrets or sensitive data.
Keep code reviewable through focused changes and stable formatting.
Refactor when structure obscures correctness, but verify behavior before and after change.
Do not optimize without evidence; do not ignore known high-impact inefficiency.
Undefined or implementation-dependent behavior can affect critical correctness.
Critical logic cannot be explained, reviewed, or tested by another qualified engineer.
Use a consistent machine-enforced style so review focuses on behavior and design.
Name concepts using the ubiquitous domain vocabulary agreed with stakeholders.
Name booleans and predicates so truth meaning is unambiguous.
Include units, time basis, currency, encoding, and coordinate system where confusion is plausible.
Distinguish identifiers, display labels, secrets, tokens, user input, and trusted values through naming and types.
Avoid abbreviations unless they are standard and unambiguous in the relevant domain.
Avoid misleading legacy names when behavior has changed.
Keep related logic physically and conceptually close.
Order code to reveal the normal flow before exceptional detail where practical.
Use early returns or structured decomposition to limit unnecessary nesting.
Avoid dense expressions that hide evaluation order, side effects, or error handling.
Replace unexplained literals with named domain concepts when meaning is not obvious.
Use comments to explain why constraints exist, including external quirks and security assumptions.
Keep documentation synchronized with behavior or remove misleading documentation.
Write error messages that identify context and action without leaking sensitive information.
Use consistent terminology across code, schemas, APIs, UI, logs, tests, and documentation.
Make public contracts readable without requiring knowledge of internal implementation.
Use examples for complex contracts and edge semantics.
Prefer clarity over cleverness, novelty, terseness, or stylistic performance.
Review readability from the perspective of a competent maintainer unfamiliar with the change.
Abstract stable domain meaning rather than superficial syntax similarity.
Define each public contract's purpose, inputs, outputs, errors, side effects, timing, ordering, ownership, and security expectations.
State preconditions, postconditions, invariants, and exceptional behavior.
Keep contracts smaller than implementations and free from unnecessary implementation detail.
Hide representation so it can evolve without changing consumers.
Use types or schemas that make invalid states difficult or impossible to represent.
Avoid boolean flags and parameter combinations whose semantics are unclear.
Prefer cohesive parameter objects or explicit variants when arguments must change together.
Prevent null, missing, sentinel, and optional values from carrying multiple ambiguous meanings.
Make mutability and ownership explicit.
Do not expose writable internal collections or mutable references unintentionally.
Keep interface segregation aligned to consumer needs.
Provide stable error categories rather than forcing consumers to parse text.
Define compatibility and versioning before publishing a contract outside one change boundary.
Test contracts independently from implementations and across every substitute.
Avoid wrapping every dependency when no policy, isolation, testability, or evolution benefit exists.
Avoid generic abstractions that erase meaningful constraints.
Document performance and resource characteristics when consumers can depend on them.
Define cancellation, timeout, retry, and idempotency semantics for remote or long-running contracts.
Retire obsolete interfaces through monitored migration rather than indefinite parallel support.
Define an error taxonomy that distinguishes validation, conflict, authorization, not-found, dependency, resource, timeout, cancellation, integrity, and internal failures.
Detect errors as close as practical to their source while handling them at the layer that has recovery context.
Do not ignore, overwrite, convert to success, or silently log-and-continue after an error that invalidates the operation.
Preserve causal context while redacting secrets and sensitive data.
Use structured error values rather than parsing human-readable strings.
Translate errors at boundaries without losing retryability, severity, and causal identity.
Fail closed for authorization, identity, privacy, safety, and integrity controls.
Avoid broad catch-all handling that masks programming defects or corrupt state.
Ensure cleanup, rollback, lock release, and cancellation occur on every exit path.
Make retries explicit, bounded, delayed, and safe for the operation.
Separate user-facing guidance from diagnostic detail.
Avoid exposing internal paths, queries, stack traces, keys, topology, or tenant information.
Treat assertion and invariant failures as defects requiring investigation, not routine user errors.
Validate external assumptions and provider responses before use.
Use defensive copies or immutable values when callers could corrupt shared state.
Bound input, recursion, allocation, loops, retries, and concurrency against resource exhaustion.
Define safe fallback and degraded behavior before failures occur.
Make partial success explicit and reconcilable.
Test error injection at every material dependency and state transition.
Monitor unexpected error classes and repeated recoveries as signals of systemic defects.
A critical operation can report success after losing, duplicating, corrupting, or failing to authorize its effect.
Errors can leave security or business invariants silently violated.
Identify every finite resource used by the code, including memory, files, sockets, connections, threads, tasks, locks, handles, subscriptions, and temporary storage.
Make resource ownership and transfer explicit.
Acquire resources as late as practical and release them as early as safe.
Use structured lifetime mechanisms so cleanup occurs on success, error, cancellation, and timeout.
Prevent double release, use-after-release, dangling references, and ownership ambiguity.
Bound pools, queues, buffers, caches, batches, and concurrency.
Set timeouts and cancellation for operations that can wait indefinitely.
Avoid holding scarce resources across user input, network calls, or long computation without justification.
Size pools from measured demand and downstream capacity rather than arbitrary defaults.
Prevent pool exhaustion from causing uncontrolled retry or cascading failure.
Clean temporary, orphaned, expired, and abandoned resources reliably.
Handle partial acquisition by releasing already-acquired resources.
Avoid unbounded object retention through listeners, closures, caches, registries, or diagnostic context.
Measure memory, allocation, handle, connection, and thread behavior under sustained load.
Test resource exhaustion and recovery.
Make spill, eviction, rejection, and load-shedding behavior explicit.
Protect shared resources from noisy neighbors.
Avoid performing cleanup that can delete another operation's or tenant's resources.
Make resource limits configurable, validated, documented, and observable.
Verify that shutdown drains, transfers, persists, or safely abandons in-flight work.
Use concurrency only where it provides required responsiveness, throughput, isolation, or latency benefit.
Define which state is shared, immutable, thread-confined, message-owned, or synchronized.
Prefer ownership transfer and immutability over shared mutation.
Protect every shared invariant with a coherent synchronization strategy.
Avoid blocking operations on event loops, cooperative schedulers, or latency-critical threads.
Bound task creation, fan-out, parallelism, queues, and in-flight work.
Propagate cancellation, deadlines, tenant context, identity, trace context, and request scope correctly.
Do not detach background work without ownership, error handling, lifecycle, and shutdown behavior.
Define ordering and completion semantics explicitly.
Prevent races between timeout, cancellation, completion, retry, and cleanup.
Avoid holding locks while invoking untrusted, remote, or reentrant code.
Use lock ordering or lock-free designs deliberately to prevent deadlock.
Protect against starvation, livelock, priority inversion, and unfair scheduling.
Make async errors observable and attributable to the initiating work.
Preserve idempotency when work can be retried or duplicated.
Test under randomized scheduling, high contention, slow dependencies, cancellation, and shutdown.
Use race detectors, deterministic schedulers, model checking, or stress tools where available and appropriate.
Document memory visibility and consistency assumptions where the execution model requires it.
Treat nondeterministic test failures as defects rather than normal noise.
Verify that parallel execution does not violate rate, quota, ordering, or downstream capacity limits.
Define a schema, type, allowed range, default, sensitivity, owner, and description for every configuration value.
Validate all configuration before serving work and fail safely on invalid critical values.
Make precedence across defaults, files, environment, remote sources, and command-line input explicit.
Avoid configuration values whose meaning changes by undocumented convention.
Do not store secrets in ordinary configuration or expose them through diagnostics.
Separate environment identity from behavior and avoid environment-name conditionals scattered through code.
Version configuration with the release or maintain equivalent auditable traceability.
Make dynamic configuration updates atomic, observable, authorized, and reversible.
Define stale-cache, unavailable-source, and partial-update behavior.
Treat flags as temporary lifecycle-managed code with owner, purpose, default, scope, creation date, and removal date.
Test both flag states and material combinations before exposure.
Use safe defaults when flag evaluation fails.
Restrict and audit high-impact flag changes.
Avoid nested flags and flag interactions that create untestable state spaces.
Remove completed rollout flags and dead branches promptly.
Do not use flags as permanent authorization, pricing, compliance, or data-isolation mechanisms without appropriate governance.
Ensure configuration changes cannot bypass validation, deployment controls, or segregation of duties.
Redact sensitive values from logs, UIs, metrics, and support tools.
Provide configuration drift detection and reconstruction.
Include configuration in incident, rollback, and reproducibility evidence.
Add a dependency only when its total lifecycle benefit exceeds implementing or avoiding the capability.
Evaluate maintainer identity, release history, support, security practice, community health, documentation, and abandonment risk.
Use trusted sources and verify package identity, namespace, signature, hash, or provenance as available.
Pin versions or constraints tightly enough to prevent unreviewed substitution.
Record direct and transitive dependencies in a machine-readable inventory.
Separate build, development, optional, and runtime dependencies.
Minimize privileged, networked, native, dynamically loaded, or executable dependencies.
Review license, notice, patent, redistribution, and source-disclosure obligations before use.
Avoid multiple libraries providing the same capability without a justified migration plan.
Wrap volatile or high-risk dependencies behind a policy boundary when replacement or containment is valuable.
Do not rely on undocumented behavior or private interfaces.
Test supported versions and upgrade paths.
Automate updates while preserving review, test, provenance, and rollback gates.
Monitor newly disclosed vulnerabilities and compromised releases after deployment.
Prioritize remediation by exploitability, reachability, exposure, impact, and controls.
Remove unused, abandoned, end-of-life, and superseded dependencies.
Maintain an emergency process to revoke, replace, rebuild, and redeploy a compromised dependency.
Track local patches and forks with ownership and upstream strategy.
Prevent dependency confusion, typosquatting, namespace collision, and untrusted install scripts.
Verify the final artifact contains only intended dependency content.
Define the problem, desired quality improvement, boundaries, risks, and measurable completion criteria.
Establish characterization tests or other evidence for current required behavior before structural change.
Distinguish required behavior from defects, accidental quirks, and obsolete compatibility.
Use small, reviewable, reversible steps with continuous verification.
Avoid mixing broad behavior change, dependency upgrade, migration, and refactoring without a clear reason.
Preserve public contracts or provide a controlled migration.
Add seams around tightly coupled or untestable areas before changing internals.
Use parallel run, shadow comparison, dual read, or reconciliation where behavior equivalence is difficult to prove.
Measure defect rate, change lead time, complexity, performance, and operational burden before and after.
Remove dead paths, compatibility shims, stale flags, and old data only after consumers have migrated.
Keep data migrations resumable and auditable.
Do not translate code mechanically into a new language or framework without reconsidering domain boundaries and failure semantics.
Prioritize high-interest debt that creates recurring incidents, vulnerability, delay, or inability to change.
Stop modernization that expands scope without reducing the target risk or cost.
Preserve historical decision context and document new constraints.
Verify rollback or safe roll-forward at each migration stage.
Avoid permanent dual systems without an owner and exit date.
Include operators, support, security, data, and users in modernization impact review.
Treat unexplained legacy behavior as an investigation target, not permission to break it.
Retire obsolete infrastructure, credentials, data, and suppliers after migration completes.
Define review objectives, required reviewers, independence, evidence, and approval rules according to risk.
Keep changes small and focused enough for reliable human review.
Provide context, requirement links, design rationale, risk, test evidence, migration, rollout, and rollback information.
Review behavior and consequences rather than formatting already enforced by tools.
Verify requirements, invariants, authorization, validation, error handling, concurrency, data, and operational behavior.
Examine deleted and generated content as well as added lines.
Check whether tests can fail for the defect they claim to detect.
Challenge assumptions, edge cases, misuse, partial failure, and recovery.
Use specialists for security, privacy, accessibility, data, cryptography, performance, or safety-sensitive changes.
Prevent authors from approving their own material changes.
Resolve review comments explicitly; do not dismiss findings through status changes without rationale.
Distinguish blocking defects, required follow-up, questions, and optional suggestions.
Re-review materially changed code after approval.
Record exceptional bypasses and perform prompt retrospective review.
Use checklists as memory aids, not substitutes for understanding.
Avoid review overload, rubber-stamping, and excessive queues through ownership and change sizing.
Measure escapes and review effectiveness rather than comment count or review speed alone.
Create automated rules from recurring objective review findings.
Maintain respectful, specific, evidence-based review communication.
Verify the merged artifact and configuration still match the reviewed change.
